Quick size guide

  • Above a sofa (single piece): Aim for 50–75% of the sofa's width. For a standard 2-metre sofa, that is roughly 100–150 cm wide. Anything narrower will look lost.
  • Above a bed (single piece or group): Width should be roughly equal to the bed width — or the headboard width if the headboard is narrower than the bed base. For a kingsize bed, 150 cm is a good starting point for a single piece.
  • Gallery wall grouping: Treat the total width of the whole arrangement as one unit and apply the same percentage rules as a single piece. The grouping should not exceed the width of the furniture below.
  • Statement wall with no furniture: You have more freedom here. A large-format piece of 90 cm or wider looks best on a wall with nothing beneath it — it can sit lower and command the whole space.
  • Small spaces and narrow walls: Resist the temptation to use small art to match a small wall. A single medium piece (60–70 cm wide) often looks far better in a small hallway than four tiny pieces that add visual noise without substance.
[[PRODUCT|large format wall art prints for statement focal wall]]
Pro Tip: Cut a piece of brown kraft paper to the exact dimensions of the art you are considering and tape it to your wall before you buy. It sounds obvious, but it is the single most effective way to test whether a size is right for your space — and it has saved more than one client from an expensive mistake.

Visual Inspiration: Gallery Wall Styles and Layouts to Explore

Sometimes the best way to decide how to arrange multiple wall art pieces is simply to see it done well in different styles. Browse the looks below for ideas that fit your own space and aesthetic.

Visual Inspiration

Explore complementary design ideas on our Home Decor by Trend page:

  • Eclectic Maximalist Home Decor Trend - bold layered gallery wall arrangements
  • Modern Contemporary Home Decor Trend - sleek curated multi-piece art displays
  • Cosy Minimalism Home Decor Trend - balanced understated wall art groupings

More About Arranging Wall Art at Home

Arranging wall art well is as much about confidence as it is about technique — and the more you understand why the rules exist, the easier it becomes to know when to follow them and when to break them.

The core principles in this guide — planning on the floor, respecting furniture proportions, keeping spacing consistent, and testing with tape before nailing — apply just as much to a single piece as they do to a gallery wall of twenty. What changes between a beginner arrangement and a genuinely beautiful one is usually just the willingness to slow down, plan properly, and make small adjustments before committing.

If you are starting from scratch and building a collection, do not feel pressured to hang everything at once. It is completely fine — and often better — to start with two or three pieces you love and add to the grouping over time as you find things that fit. The best-looking walls are rarely the ones that were planned all at once from a matching set.

WATCH: Arrange Your Art Into A Gallery Wall

Ready to Try It Yourself?

Arranging multiple wall art pieces does not have to be stressful or expensive — it just needs a plan, a bit of painter's tape, and the willingness to shuffle things around until they feel right. Take it one step at a time: start on the floor, photograph what you like, tape it to the wall, and only then reach for the hammer.

Your wall does not need to be perfect from day one. Some of the most beautiful rooms I have ever worked in started with just two prints and a bit of instinct, and grew into something really special over time. Trust your eye — you probably know more than you think you do.

So tell me: do you have a particular wall you have been putting off tackling, or a grouping that is not quite working yet? I would love to hear what you are working with and help you figure out the best approach.

Knowing how to arrange multiple wall art pieces is one of those skills that transforms a room from "fine" to genuinely impressive — and the good news is that it is far more straightforward than most people think once you have a simple system to follow.

By Mae Osz | Interior Design Consultant & Home Decor Expert with 12+ years of experience.

Have you ever stood in front of a blank wall, four or five pieces of wall art leaning against your skirting boards, and had absolutely no idea where to begin? I have been there — and so has almost every client I have ever worked with. That feeling of overwhelm is real, but it disappears the moment you have a proper plan.

Quick answer: To arrange multiple wall art pieces well, plan your layout on the floor or with paper templates before anything goes on the wall, follow the 57–60 inch eye-level rule for hanging height, and use consistent spacing (typically 2–4 inches between frames) to keep the grouping feeling intentional rather than cluttered.

Arranging several pieces together is really about creating visual harmony — a sense that the wall has been curated rather than randomly filled. Whether you are pulling together a full gallery wall or simply hanging a pair of prints above a sideboard, the same core principles apply. If you are searching for unique wall art to build your grouping from scratch, or browsing for unique home decor to complement your display, having a clear arrangement strategy means you will shop with confidence rather than guessing.

How to Plan Your Layout Before Hanging

The single best thing you can do when arranging multiple wall art pieces is to plan everything before a single nail goes in. I always tell clients: the wall is the last place you should figure this out. Start on the floor.

Step-by-step planning method

  • Lay everything on the floor first. Place all your pieces on the floor in front of the wall where they will hang. Shuffle them around until you find a composition you like — it costs nothing and takes five minutes.
  • Trace paper templates. Place each frame face-down on a sheet of brown kraft paper or newspaper and trace around it. Cut out the shapes and label them so you know which piece is which.
  • Mark the hanging hardware. With the frame still face-down on the paper template, mark exactly where the hook or wire falls. This tells you precisely where the nail goes without measuring twice.
  • Use the floor arrangement as your map. Once you are happy with the layout on the floor, photograph it on your phone. That image is your reference when you move to the wall.
  • Measure the total footprint. Use a tape measure to note the overall width and height of your arrangement so you can position the whole group correctly on the wall.

I once helped a client in Bristol who had been trying to hang a gallery wall of nine prints for three weeks. Every weekend she would put a few nails in, step back, hate it, and fill the holes. The moment we laid everything on the floor and photographed the arrangement, the whole job was done in under an hour. The floor is your friend.

Pro Tip: Keep a 2 cm border of open wall space around the whole arrangement before you finalise the position — this stops the grouping looking crammed into a corner and gives it room to breathe.

How to Arrange Art Above Furniture

Hanging art above furniture is probably the most common scenario I am asked about, and there is a simple formula that works every single time. The art should feel connected to the furniture beneath it — not floating off into space, and not crushing down on top of it.

Furniture-specific hanging rules

Furniture Piece Ideal Gap Above Width Guideline Notes
Sofa 15–20 cm (6–8 inches) 50–75% of sofa width Never wider than the sofa; centre visually
Bed headboard 10–15 cm (4–6 inches) Up to full bed width Lower feels more intimate and cosy
Console table 15–25 cm (6–10 inches) 60–80% of table width Layer objects on table to anchor the art
Fireplace mantel 8–15 cm (3–6 inches) Fill the chimney breast width Lean art for a relaxed, flexible look
Sideboard / dresser 15–20 cm (6–8 inches) 50–70% of furniture width Mix heights of art and objects on surface

The most common mistake I see above a sofa is art that is hung far too high. People worry about knocking their heads — which is a reasonable instinct — but the result is a piece that looks completely disconnected from the sofa below. When in doubt, go lower than feels comfortable. It almost always looks better.


SHOP HERE
Pro Tip: When arranging multiple pieces above a fireplace, treat the whole chimney breast as one canvas. Keep the outer edges of your arrangement inside the chimney breast width — going wider makes it feel chaotic rather than considered.

How to Create a Gallery Wall

A gallery wall is the most exciting way to arrange multiple wall art pieces, and it is far less scary than it looks on Instagram. The key is choosing your layout style first — and there are really only three main types.

The three gallery wall styles

  • Grid layout: All frames the same size, evenly spaced in rows and columns. Clean, modern, and very easy to execute. Works brilliantly in a minimal or Scandi-style home.
  • Organic layout: A mix of frame sizes and orientations clustered around a central "anchor" piece. This is the most personal and creative style but needs the most planning time on the floor first.
  • Symmetrical layout: A larger central piece flanked by matching or mirrored pairs. Easier to get right than organic, and works well in more traditional or classic interiors.

When a client tells me they want a gallery wall but are worried it will look messy, I always steer them toward the symmetrical layout to start. It has the same impact as an organic arrangement but is far more forgiving if one piece is slightly off-centre.


SHOP HERE
Real Example: I styled a narrow terrace hallway with a symmetrical gallery wall using one large landscape print in the centre and four smaller square prints arranged two on each side. The whole thing measured just 90 cm wide, but it looked like a proper curated display rather than a narrow corridor.

How to Hang Art in Pairs, Trios, and Small Groupings

Not every arrangement needs to be a full gallery wall. Sometimes two or three pieces grouped together is exactly the right answer — and small groupings have their own rules that are worth knowing.

Tips for small groupings

  • Pairs: Hang two pieces side by side with 5–8 cm between them, treating their combined width as one unit. For a vertical pair, stagger them slightly for interest, or align their centres for a formal look.
  • Trios: The classic arrangement is a larger central piece with two smaller pieces flanking it at equal height — or three equal-sized pieces in a horizontal row. Both work; choose based on your wall shape.
  • Odd numbers win: Groupings of three, five, or seven almost always look more natural and visually interesting than even numbers. If you have four pieces, consider whether one could be replaced with a small plant or sculptural object to break the symmetry.
  • Keep a consistent centre line: For horizontal groupings, align pieces along a shared centre line (imaginary horizontal axis through the middle of the group) so they read as one composition.
  • Mind the negative space: The space between and around pieces is as important as the pieces themselves. Too little space and it looks crammed; too much and they feel disconnected.

SHOP HERE
Pro Tip: When hanging a trio of different-sized pieces, place the largest in the centre and balance the two smaller ones on either side by eye rather than by measurement — your eye is usually a better judge than a ruler for irregular groupings.

Spacing and Height Rules for Arranging Multiple Pieces Together

This is the section where most people go wrong, and it is completely understandable — the numbers feel arbitrary until you understand why they exist. Getting spacing and height right is what separates a wall that looks deliberate from one that looks like an afterthought.

The key numbers to remember

  • Eye level centre height: 145–152 cm (57–60 inches) from the floor to the centre of a single piece or the visual centre of your whole grouping. This is the gallery standard and it works in almost every room.
  • Gap between frames: 5–8 cm (2–3 inches) for a cohesive grouping that reads as one arrangement. Go up to 10 cm maximum before pieces start to feel disconnected.
  • Gap above furniture: 15–20 cm (6–8 inches) between the top of the furniture and the bottom of the lowest frame in your arrangement.
  • Measure to the centre, not the top. Always measure to where the centre of the frame will sit — not to the top of the frame or the top of the hook.
  • Adjust for seating rooms: In living rooms and bedrooms where most viewing happens while seated, dropping the grouping by 5–8 cm from standard eye level often looks even better.
Pro Tip: Write your chosen centre height on a strip of painter's tape and stick it horizontally across the wall as a guide line before you start. It takes 30 seconds and means every frame lands in exactly the right place.

Room-by-Room Arrangement Guides

The rules for arranging multiple wall art pieces do not change dramatically between rooms, but the mood, the furniture anchor points, and the viewing distance all differ — and those differences matter. Here is how I approach each main room.

Room-specific arrangement tips

  • Living room: The focal wall (usually behind or opposite the sofa) is your main canvas. Plan for viewing from a seated position — that changes your ideal height slightly lower than standing eye level. A larger grouping or a statement single piece works here because the room gives you plenty of viewing distance.
  • Bedroom: Above the headboard is the natural anchor point. Keep the arrangement wide enough to relate to the bed width but avoid going wider than the bed frame itself. Calm, cohesive colour palettes work best here as you want the room to feel restful.
  • Hallway: Narrow hallways suit vertical groupings or a linear row of prints at eye level. Because people move through rather than sit in a hallway, you can use slightly bolder, more graphic pieces than you might elsewhere — they only need to work for a glance, not prolonged viewing.
  • Home office: Keep the arrangement behind or beside your desk rather than directly behind your screen if you video call — a wall that is too busy can be distracting on camera. A small, tight grouping of three to five pieces on a side wall is usually the perfect solution.
  • Dining room: A large-scale arrangement or a statement single piece works well here, ideally at seated eye level (around 130–135 cm to centre) since most time in a dining room is spent seated.
  • Children's room: Go lower — hang art at the child's eye level and do not be afraid to use brightly coloured or playful pieces that you would not necessarily choose elsewhere in the house.

SHOP HERE
Real Example: I recently worked with a family in Leeds whose hallway was extremely narrow — barely 80 cm wide. Instead of a gallery wall, we hung five small square prints in a single vertical column on the end wall, spaced 6 cm apart. It drew the eye down the hallway and made the space feel intentional rather than cramped.

SHOP HERE

Printable and Downloadable Layout Templates

One of the gaps I see most often in advice about arranging multiple wall art pieces is the absence of a practical starting point. Most people know they should plan on paper — but doing it from scratch is still fiddly. Layout templates solve that.

How to make and use your own templates

  • Start with your wall dimensions. Measure your wall width and height and note them down. Your arrangement should cover no more than two-thirds of the wall width for a balanced look.
  • Scale it down on paper. Use 1 cm to represent 10 cm of real space (a 1:10 scale). Draw your wall as a rectangle on plain paper and cut out small paper rectangles to represent each frame at scale.
  • Try the common templates above. The four layouts in the infographic cover about 90% of real-world gallery wall situations — start with whichever feels closest to your vision and adapt from there.
  • Download and print. There are free printable gallery wall templates widely available from home decor blogs and design tools — search for "gallery wall layout planner" and you will find several in common standard sizes. Print at A4 and use it as your physical planning sheet.
  • Keep your template on your phone. Photograph your chosen layout before you move to the wall so you have an instant reference without having to remember it.
Pro Tip: If you are using an organic or irregular layout, sketch the arrangement on squared paper once you are happy with it on the floor. Note the gap measurements between pieces. That sketch is worth more than any template because it is specific to your exact frames.

How to Mix Different Frame Styles, Sizes, and Orientations Cohesively

Mixing frames is where a lot of people get nervous, but it is also where the most interesting walls come from. The secret is to give your grouping at least one strong unifying element — usually colour, finish, or subject matter — and let everything else vary freely.

Mixing frames without it looking chaotic

  • Unify by frame finish: Mix frame shapes and sizes but keep all frames in the same finish family — all black, all natural wood, all brass, all white. This is the simplest and most reliable way to make an eclectic mix look intentional.
  • Vary orientation freely: Landscape, portrait, and square pieces can all live together happily in the same grouping. Variety of orientation actually adds energy and stops a wall feeling static.
  • Use size contrast deliberately: A large piece anchors the grouping; medium and small pieces fill around it. Avoid having too many pieces of identical size — it looks like a school corridor rather than a curated display.
  • Mix thick and thin frames: A chunky deep frame next to a thin-profile frame creates lovely depth variation. Try to balance the visual weight across the whole arrangement — do not put all your heavy frames on one side.
  • Try a "two-frame-style" rule: If you want to mix frame finishes, limit yourself to two. Black and natural wood together, for example, almost always works. Three different frame finishes tends to look restless.

SHOP HERE
Pro Tip: If your frames are truly all over the place and nothing is tying them together, a tin of spray paint in one colour is the fastest fix I know. Matte black is forgiving and works with almost any decor style.

Colour and Theme Cohesion Tips When Grouping Multiple Art Pieces

You can have a beautifully planned layout and perfectly spaced frames, but if the art itself does not feel like it belongs together, the wall will still look random. Colour and theme cohesion is the invisible glue that makes a grouping feel curated.

How to build cohesion across multiple pieces

  • Pull a colour from your room: Identify one or two accent colours already in your space — a cushion, a rug, a plant pot — and choose art that includes those same tones. The connection between the art and the room will feel immediate and deliberate.
  • Stick to a palette, not a perfect match: Artwork does not need to match your wall or furniture exactly. Instead, aim for a shared colour temperature — cool-toned pieces together, or warm-toned together — and the grouping will feel unified even if the individual colours vary.
  • Choose a loose theme: This does not mean every piece has to be from the same series. "Nature-inspired," "abstract shapes," "black and white photography," or "coastal scenes" are all loose enough to allow variety but specific enough to give the wall a sense of narrative.
  • Use a consistent mat (mount) width: If your pieces have different frame sizes but all share the same off-white or cream mat border, they will read as a coherent set regardless of size or subject.
  • Trust the edit: If one piece in your planned grouping consistently looks wrong when you lay everything on the floor, it probably does not belong in this particular arrangement. Be willing to set it aside for a different wall.

SHOP HERE
Pro Tip: Take a photo of your room on your phone, then hold your artwork choices up against the screen to check how they interact with your existing colour palette before you commit to a purchase. It is surprisingly accurate.

Common Mistakes to Avoid When Arranging Multiple Wall Art Pieces

After more than a decade of helping people with their walls, I have seen the same mistakes come up again and again. None of them are hard to fix once you know what to look for — and most of them are very easy to avoid from the start.

Mistakes I see most often — and how to fix them

  • Hanging everything too high. This is the number one mistake, bar none. Art that floats near the ceiling looks disconnected from the room and the furniture below. Bring it down to 57–60 inches to the centre of the arrangement and trust the result.
  • Using pieces that are too small for the wall. A single A4-sized print on a large wall looks lost. If you are going to hang small pieces, group them so the overall arrangement fills the space appropriately.
  • Ignoring the furniture below. Art does not exist in isolation — it needs to relate to what is beneath it. Always consider the furniture anchor point when planning your arrangement.
  • Too many different frame finishes. I touched on this earlier, but it is worth repeating: more than two frame finishes in one grouping usually reads as cluttered rather than curated.
  • Spacing that is inconsistent. Even if each gap is only slightly different, the eye picks it up and it makes the whole arrangement feel sloppy. Measure every gap and keep it consistent.
  • Not photographing the floor arrangement first. You will forget exactly where everything was the moment you start hanging. Photo first, always.
  • Going too matchy-matchy. On the other end of the scale, buying a "matching set of three prints" in identical frames and identical sizes can look a little flat. Add one different element — size, orientation, or a slight colour variation — to give the grouping some life.
Real Example: A client once showed me photos of her living room wall and I could not immediately identify what was wrong. Then I noticed: every single piece was the same A4 size, same black frame, same 10 cm gap, in a perfectly straight row. It looked like signage rather than art. We swapped one piece for a larger A3 version of a similar print and immediately the whole row had a focal point. One change, completely different feel.

How to Use Painter's Tape to Test Arrangements Before Nailing

This is hands-down the most practical technique I teach every client, and it costs almost nothing. Using painter's tape on the wall to test your arrangement means you can live with a layout for a few days before committing a single nail to your plaster.

Step-by-step tape-testing method

  • Use low-tack painter's tape only. This is critical — regular masking tape or sellotape can pull paint when removed. Blue painter's tape is designed to come off cleanly.
  • Use your paper templates. Tape the cut-out paper templates directly to the wall rather than just outlining the frames with tape. This gives you a much better sense of the actual visual weight of each piece.
  • Mark the hanging point. On each template, make a small mark through the template at the exact spot where the nail will go. When you are ready to hang, the mark is already on the wall.
  • Step back and live with it. Leave the templates on the wall for a day or two and look at them in different lights — morning light, evening lamplight, overcast daylight. You will spot any adjustments before anything is permanent.
  • Photograph it. As with the floor arrangement, photograph the taped layout on your phone so you have a reference when you start hanging the actual frames.
  • Remove cleanly. Peel the tape back slowly at a low angle to the wall. It should come off without leaving any residue or lifting paint if it is genuine painter's tape.

I tried this method for the first time on my own sitting room wall and genuinely could not believe how useful it was. I had been planning to hang a large piece on the left of the arrangement, but once I had the template up, I could see immediately that it needed to be on the right to balance the dark sofa beneath it. I would never have noticed that just from measuring.

Pro Tip: If you live in a rented property, the tape-testing method is doubly useful — you can plan and refine your arrangement thoroughly before making any holes, and minimise the total number of nails you need to put in.

SHOP HERE

How to Choose Wall Art Style

When people ask me how to choose wall art style, I always start with the same question: what do you want to feel in this room? The style of art you choose should reinforce the mood you are trying to create — it is one of the fastest ways to shift the atmosphere of a space.

Matching art style to room mood

  • Calm and restful (bedroom, reading nook): Soft botanical prints, watercolour landscapes, or abstract line art in muted tones — sage, dusty pink, warm cream. Avoid high-contrast or visually busy pieces in spaces where you want to unwind.
  • Energising and sociable (living room, dining room): Bolder colours, graphic shapes, photography, or expressive abstract work. These rooms can handle more visual energy because you are awake and active in them.
  • Creative and playful (home office, studio): Typography, illustrated maps, architectural drawings, or graphic art that sparks thinking. The key is pieces that feel interesting to look at repeatedly, since you spend long stretches in these rooms.
  • Minimal and sophisticated: Large-scale black-and-white photography or simple line drawings in thin frames. Less is more — one strong piece often does more than five smaller ones in a minimal interior.
  • Warm and characterful (hallway, snug): Portraits, vintage prints, mixed-media pieces, or photography with a storytelling quality. These are spaces for personality.

SHOP HERE
Pro Tip: Do not feel pressured to match your art style to a single interior trend. The most interesting homes I visit always have one or two unexpected pieces that break the expected style — a bold abstract in an otherwise classic room, or a vintage botanical print in a modern minimal space. That contrast is what gives a home character.

How to Create a Focal Point in a Room

Every well-designed room has a focal point — the thing your eye goes to first when you walk in the door. Learning how to create a focal point in a room using art is one of the most powerful tools in a decorator's kit, and it is something anyone can do without a renovation budget.

How to establish a visual focal point with art

  • Choose the dominant wall first. In a living room this is usually the wall opposite the main entrance, or the chimney breast wall. In a bedroom it is almost always the wall behind the headboard. Work with the room's existing architecture.
  • Go bigger than feels comfortable. The most common error when trying to create a focal point is using art that is too small. A large-scale piece — or a gallery wall that covers a significant portion of the wall — has the visual weight to actually become a focal point.
  • Use contrast. A dark piece on a light wall, or a bold colour piece in a neutral room, creates instant contrast that draws the eye. Even the frame can contribute — a substantial frame on a minimal piece increases its visual presence enormously.
  • Anchor it with furniture and lighting. A focal point works best when it is supported by the furniture arrangement (sofa or bed pointing toward it) and by lighting — a picture light above, or a lamp positioned to wash light across the wall, adds drama and draws the eye even more effectively.
  • Limit competition. Once you have established your focal point, resist filling every other wall equally. Supporting walls should feel secondary — lighter, calmer, or sparser — so the focal point can do its job.
Real Example: I visited a client whose open-plan living and dining room felt like it had no centre of gravity — the eye did not know where to rest. We painted the chimney breast a deep inky blue and mounted a large round mirror above the fireplace. Within a day of that one change, the whole room felt anchored. Sometimes creating a focal point is about giving the wall permission to be bold.

What Size Wall Art Do I Need?

"What size wall art do I need?" is one of the questions I am asked most often, and the answer depends on three things: the size of your wall, the furniture beneath or around the art, and whether you are hanging one piece or multiple pieces as a group.

Quick size guide

  • Above a sofa (single piece): Aim for 50–75% of the sofa's width. For a standard 2-metre sofa, that is roughly 100–150 cm wide. Anything narrower will look lost.
  • Above a bed (single piece or group): Width should be roughly equal to the bed width — or the headboard width if the headboard is narrower than the bed base. For a kingsize bed, 150 cm is a good starting point for a single piece.
  • Gallery wall grouping: Treat the total width of the whole arrangement as one unit and apply the same percentage rules as a single piece. The grouping should not exceed the width of the furniture below.
  • Statement wall with no furniture: You have more freedom here. A large-format piece of 90 cm or wider looks best on a wall with nothing beneath it — it can sit lower and command the whole space.
  • Small spaces and narrow walls: Resist the temptation to use small art to match a small wall. A single medium piece (60–70 cm wide) often looks far better in a small hallway than four tiny pieces that add visual noise without substance.

It sounds obvious, but it is the single most effective way to test whether a size is right for your space — and it has saved more than one client from an expensive mistake.

More About Arranging Wall Art at Home

Arranging wall art well is as much about confidence as it is about technique — and the more you understand why the rules exist, the easier it becomes to know when to follow them and when to break them.

The core principles in this guide — planning on the floor, respecting furniture proportions, keeping spacing consistent, and testing with tape before nailing — apply just as much to a single piece as they do to a gallery wall of twenty. What changes between a beginner arrangement and a genuinely beautiful one is usually just the willingness to slow down, plan properly, and make small adjustments before committing.

If you are starting from scratch and building a collection, do not feel pressured to hang everything at once. It is completely fine — and often better — to start with two or three pieces you love and add to the grouping over time as you find things that fit. The best-looking walls are rarely the ones that were planned all at once from a matching set.

Ready to Try It Yourself?

Arranging multiple wall art pieces does not have to be stressful or expensive — it just needs a plan, a bit of painter's tape, and the willingness to shuffle things around until they feel right. Take it one step at a time: start on the floor, photograph what you like, tape it to the wall, and only then reach for the hammer.

Your wall does not need to be perfect from day one. Some of the most beautiful rooms I have ever worked in started with just two prints and a bit of instinct, and grew into something really special over time. Trust your eye — you probably know more than you think you do.
